title: Dynamic programming for 0-1 knapsack
summary: With three items that may each be chosen at most once, this example steps cell by cell through the 0-1 knapsack recurrence and finds a maximum total value of 20 at capacity 4.
context: There are 3 candidate items (n = 3), whose IDs, names, weights, and values are given in the input table. With knapsack capacity cap = 4, the goal is to maximize total value without exceeding capacity; the knapsack need not be filled completely.

State dp[i, c] denotes the maximum value obtainable from the first i items with total weight at most capacity c. Row index i runs from 0 to 3 and column index c runs from 0 to 4, forming a 4-row by 5-column state table; item IDs i start at 1 and correspond to array weight wgt[i-1] and value val[i-1].
description: Step 1 initializes the table; steps 2 to 5, 6 to 9, and 10 to 13 compute rows 1, 2, and 3 across capacities c = 1 to 4; step 14 returns the answer. Each non-boundary cell is computed once and never modified afterward. Cells in the final table include the step number at which they are first computed: before that step, a cell holds the uncomputed initial value 0; from that step onward, it holds the final value shown in the table.

For item i, write w for its weight and v for its value. If w > c, the item does not fit and must be excluded, inheriting dp[i-1, c] directly above; otherwise compare dp[i-1, c] (excluding it) with dp[i-1, c-w] + v (including it), found in the previous row shifted w columns to the left. Both sources come from the previous row, which has not yet included item i, ensuring each item is chosen at most once.

frames.title: Initialize the 4×5 state matrix
frames.explanation: Create a 4-row by 5-column dp table filled initially with 0. Row 0 (no items) and column 0 (zero capacity) hold settled boundary values of 0, shown in dark text in the figure; the remaining 12 cells hold uncomputed initial values of 0, shown in faint text, and must not be read as computed optimal values.
frames.key_state: Initialize the 4×5 dp table to all 0: the first row and first column are valid boundaries of 0, while the other 12 cells hold uncomputed initial values of 0.
frames.announcement: Initialize the 4×5 dp matrix and set the no-item first row and zero-capacity first column boundaries to 0.

frames.title: Compute dp[1, 1], getting 5
frames.explanation: Consider only the first item at capacity 1, where the current item is the apple (weight 1, value 5). Excluding it gives dp[0, 1] = 0 from the previous row; including it leaves capacity 1 - 1 = 0, looks up dp[0, 0] = 0 in the previous row (the first 0 items), and adds value 5 to get 5. Take the larger value 5 and write it to dp[1, 1]. Before this cell lie only the initialized boundary cells, and later non-boundary cells still hold uncomputed initial values of 0.
frames.key_state: Only the first item (apple), capacity 1: include the apple, setting dp[1, 1] to 5; later non-boundary cells still hold uncomputed initial values of 0.
frames.announcement: Compute dp[1, 1] (the first item only, capacity 1): including the apple beats excluding it, so write maximum value 5.

frames.title: Return maximum value 20 for capacity 4

The final frame's note "Return the maximum achievable knapsack value after considering all items: 20" means the optimal subset chosen from all three candidate items; packing all three would weigh 6, exceeding capacity 4.
